info.bio:
Kraftwerk (central eléctrica) es un grupo alemán de música de vanguardia que hizo una contribución decisiva al desarrollo de la música electrónica.

El grupo lo formaron Ralf Hütter y Florian Schneider en 1970, pero su fama la hicieron como cuarteto, con Wolfgang Flür y Karl Bartos.

Las técnicas que introdujeron en su música, así como el equipo que desarrollaron, son hoy omnipresentes en la música moderna ya que son considerados por muchos como los padres de la música electrónica que si bien ya venia de tiempo atrás

own_scenes.desc: En el hueco de comienzos de los ochenta, entre el final del disco y los monolitos de Michael Jackson y Madonna, cuando «new wave» lo englobaba todo y, como dice Alan Oldham, a los chicos negros no se les penalizaba por escuchar rock, el austero grupo alemán se volvió el eslabón con el techno y el house. Desde Autobahn (1974) sacó la electrónica de los laboratorios y la metió en el pop: no una sinfonía de rock progresivo, sino «una canción pop muy larga». Con Trans-Europe Express (1977) y Computer World (1981) llegó un sonido de máquina perfecta, «tan rígido que es funky». Con la sección rítmica de Karl Bartos y Wolfgang Flür se acercó al soul: eran fans de Motown y James Brown, «ritmo americano con armonía europea», y en «Tour de France» (1983) los pedales y cadenas de bicicleta suenan como la guitarra de Jimmy Nolen. «Planet Rock» bebe de ellos, el house de Chicago cita «Home Computer» y el techno de Detroit los portamentos de «Numbers». De ahí la frase de Derrick May que la prensa europea convirtió en definición: George Clinton y Kraftwerk atrapados en un ascensor. Sicko advierte que simplifica: muchas influencias del techno vienen del propio Detroit.

influences.name: Motown, P-Funk y el funk del Medio Oeste

refs.q: Clean, syncopated rhythms propelled Kraftwerk’s sound into the realm of dance music, described by many American listeners as “so stiff it’s funky.”
refs.para: By the time Kraftwerk recorded Trans-Europe Express in 1977 and Computer World in 1981, its meticulousness in the studio was reflected in a much-imitated straight-laced appearance and a seamless, machine-perfect sound. Clean, syncopated rhythms propelled Kraftwerk’s sound into the realm of dance music, described by many American listeners as “so stiff it’s funky.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 1: Welcome to the Machine: America Wakes Up to Techno, 1997–2010

refs.q: We always tried to make an American rhythm feel, with a European approach to harmony and melody.
refs.para: Just as critics were beginning to understand the Beach Boys’ influence on vocal harmonies in the Autobahn album, Kraftwerk’s love of soul and dance music started to significantly work its way into the group’s music. As former Kraftwerk member Karl Bartos explains, “We were all fans of American music: soul, the whole Tamla/Motown thing, and of course James Brown. We always tried to make an American rhythm feel, with a European approach to harmony and melody.” This combination is audible at least as far back as “Trans-Europe Express” in 1977, but is most pronounced in the group’s 1983 hit single “Tour de France.” Probably Kraftwerk’s most explicit and visceral emulation of a real-world object, “Tour de France” bases its rhythm around the chain, pedal, and gear sounds of bicycles. Intentionally or otherwise, the metallic gliding and ticking of these sounds recalls the tight, rhythmic guitar work of Jimmy Nolen on James Brown staples like “Cold Sweat.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 1: Welcome to the Machine: America Wakes Up to Techno, 1997–2010

refs.q: It’s like George Clinton and Kraftwerk stuck in an elevator.
refs.para: Many historical reconstructions of techno’s past name Kraftwerk and funk music as the sole influences on early techno. Perhaps it was this quote from techno pioneer Derrick May that set the precedent for this connection: “The music [techno] is just like Detroit—a complete mistake. It’s like George Clinton and Kraftwerk stuck in an elevator.” If only May could collect royalties on this sound bite! Intended as an off-the-cuff remark, it was quickly snapped up by the European press and has been used as a textbook definition for techno ever since. But while it’s true that Kraftwerk had a far-reaching effect on electronic music as a whole, this simplification ignores techno’s complex range of influences, many of which came not from Germany but from the Midwestern American city of Detroit.

scenes.name: Afrika Bambaataa y la Zulu Nation
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Lance Taylor, antiguo miembro de los Black Spades, reunió los elementos de la cultura (DJ, MC, graffiti y b-boying) en una sola comunidad, inspirado por la unidad del pueblo zulú: exmiembros de bandas convertidos en DJs, MCs, bailarines y grafiteros. Pinchaba en el centro comunitario de Bronx River y en el T-Connection de Ritchie T, rodeado de cajas de discos como «una caravana y la entrada de una banda». El «Maestro de los discos» lo mezclaba todo: rock duro, funk, clásica, go-go, música haitiana, salsa, la sintonía de Mi bella genio o «Mary, Mary» de los Monkees. De la Zulu Nation salieron los Jazzy Five y la Soulsonic Force; en los ochenta la Universal Zulu Nation llevó el hip hop por el mundo, de Japón a Sudáfrica, y le añadió un quinto elemento: el conocimiento.
scenes.family: Old school: DJs, MCs y fiestas del Bronx

scenes.name: Afrika Bambaataa y el electro-funk
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El instigador del electro-funk y del movimiento hip hop mundial, «una amenaza para el sistema»: DJ del Bronx con nombre zulú, líder de la Zulu Nation (breakdancers, grafiteros, DJ y MC). «Planet Rock» (Tommy Boy, 1982), con bajo atronador y sintetizadores espaciales, lanzó el sonido Tommy Boy (Jonzun Crew, Planet Patrol) e influyó en el house de Chicago, el bass de Miami y Egyptian Lover. Con «Renegades of Funk» (1983) mezcló cantos africanos y presentó a la Soul Sonic Force como superhéroes a lo Dr. Funkenstein; agradecía a Sly, Clinton, Bootsy y James Brown, con quien grabó «Unity» (1984) antes de que todos samplearan a Brown. Influyó en Jungle Brothers, Public Enemy, X-Clan o De La Soul. The Light (1988), con Clinton, Bootsy, Yellowman, UB40 y Boy George, era su visión de liberación global; Capitol lo recortó a un disco y fracasó. El padrino del hip hop.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: Funk industrial
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: Krautrock y motorik
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Los ritmos «motorik» teutónicos de Kraftwerk y Neu! y la improvisación disciplinada de Can. Para muchos postpunks el single más significativo de 1977 no fue «White Riot» sino «Trans-Europe Express», canto fúnebre metronómico para la era industrial: una visión de la Neue Europa moderna, auténticamente postrock, sin deuda con la música estadounidense.
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Krautrock: Cluster, Kraftwerk, Faust y Neu!
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Sin interés por la psicodelia ni por el universo, fascinados morbosamente por la psique del siglo XX. Kluster/Cluster pasan de la disonancia electrónica a los drones y al ambient (Zuckerzeit, Harmonia, Grosses Wasser); Kraftwerk funden electrónica, sonido industrial y melodía pop, sustituyen la batería por ritmos electrónicos y engendran a la vez la música industrial y la disco (Autobahn); Faust, el primer grupo «lo-fi», collages expresionistas y una de las visiones más líricas de la alienación moderna; Neu!, el «motorik beat» de Klaus Dinger y la repetición obsesiva.

scenes.name: Música disco
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El funk abre la puerta a la subcultura disco: los gays de Nueva York, perseguidos, crean sus islas sociales en clubes privados y recuperan la despersonalización del éxtasis colectivo. Tres hechos la impulsan: el soul orquestal de Barry White, «Autobahn» de Kraftwerk y el Polymoog. Manu Dibango («Soul Makossa») y MFSB la inventan; Giorgio Moroder casa la música robótica de Kraftwerk con el soul (Donna Summer, «I Feel Love», nacimiento del synth-pop). Van McCoy, el maxi de 12" de Walter Gibbons, Chic, Grace Jones, Gloria Gaynor, Saturday Night Fever, el Warehouse de Frankie Knuckles y el Paradise Garage de Larry Levan. Los reyes del pop: Michael Jackson (Thriller, «el mayor farol de todos los tiempos») y Prince, su contrapartida intelectual.

scenes.name: Los clubes sociales de instituto: Charivari, Gables y las fiestas «prep»
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: En el Detroit vaciado de finales de los setenta, sin discotecas juveniles y con el Renaissance Center y Trapper’s Alley como sustitutos fallidos, los alumnos de los institutos del noroeste se organizaron en «party clubs», casi todos masculinos y elitistas, que contrataban DJs, luces y salas: Plush, Funtime Society, Universal y GQ Productions primero, y luego decenas con nombres de tiendas o diseñadores italianos (Giavante, Ciabittino, Schiaparelli, Remnique, Cacharel…), vestidos de Max Julien, botas Roots y Fiorucci. Kevin Bledsoe montó Charivari con su hermano Brian (por una tienda neoyorquina) y Todd Johnson, con su empresa de sonido y DJs Direct Drive, fundó Gables («si os perdéis nuestras fiestas, francamente, os importa un bledo») y soñó con un supercártel de clubes. Fiestas de 400 a 1.200 chavales, sin adultos, en el tercer piso del Women’s City Club (Park Avenue Club), con A Flock of Seagulls en el segundo y el Detroit Jazz Center en el primero. La división entre «preps» del noroeste y «jits» de la calle (y el baile jit) se disolvió hacia 1982-1983 con los coches y los clubes del este (Climax, Club UBQ), más funkies y mezclados: de «dress to impress» a «dress to sweat». A finales de 1983 la violencia y los tiroteos acabaron con la escena.

scenes.name: Kraftwerk y el synth-pop pionero
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: Kraftwerk tuvo la idea que llevaría la electrónica al gran público: usar la paleta del sintetizador para canciones pop pegadizas como «Autobahn».

scenes.name: Electroclash / revival ochentero
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: Los revivals de los noventa no son mero mimetismo: Thomas P. Heckmann rellena la EBM de acid; Chicks on Speed vuelven a la new wave con portátiles; Playgroup al avant-funk. El sello International Deejay Gigolo de DJ Hell (Miss Kittin & The Hacker, Zombie Nation) resucita el glam electrónico, el synth-pop y el electro sadomaso; Daniel Wang y Environ, el computer disco de Moroder. «Sounds good… feels good too» (Fischerspooner).

podcast.title: Founding as a Personal Project (1970)
podcast.body: Crabwork originated as the personal endeavor of two individuals, Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider. Their collaboration began prior to 1970, with existing recordings from that year showing them performing together in a very similar precursor project. They also signed some early Crabwork material as just the two of them. "Crabwork realmente es el proyecto personal de dos personas, de Ralph y de Florian, que empezaron a trabajar juntos, de hecho tenemos ya grabaciones de antes en 1970."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: German Identity in Music (1974)
podcast.body: Hailing from Dusseldorf, Kraftwerk aimed to create a sound that would distinguish Germany musically from the rest of the world. They drew upon Germany's long history of electronic music experimentation, referencing an electronic studio opened in Cologne in 1951. "They were from Dusseldorf in what was then West Germany. And they were part of a generation of musicians who were looking for a sound that would set Germany apart from the rest of the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Synthesizer and Rhythm Machine Mastery (1975)
podcast.body: By 1975, Kraftwerk was already extensively using synthesizers and rhythm machines to create sounds that contained elements of many future music styles. Their innovative use of these instruments showcased the potential for electronic music to evolve into diverse forms. "you can hear all the elements of all sorts of future music in what craftwork was doing with their synthesizers and rhythm machines as far back as 1975."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transformative Live Performance (September 11, 1975)
podcast.body: Andy McCluskey of OMD saw Kraftwerk perform at the Liverpool Empire on this date, an event he credits with transforming his life and inspiring OMD's musical direction. Paul Humphreys, being 15, was unable to attend due to his mother's rules. "I went to go and see Kraftwerk play at the Liverpool Empire on September the 11th, 1975. And that transformed my life."

podcast.title: Pioneering Technological Innovation (1976)
podcast.body: Kraftwerk, known for commissioning custom machines, spurred a significant technological advance in 1976 by tasking the sound engineering company Matten & Wiechers with developing the Syntanorma sequencer, a pivotal moment in music history. "En 1976 Grabbar hizo un avance tecnológico en la música que cambiaría la música para siempre."

podcast.title: Influential After 1977
podcast.body: Kraftwerk is considered by some to be the most influential band in the world next to The Beatles, with their impact traceable in music starting anytime after 1977. Their influence spans EDM, techno (including Detroit techno and Daft Punk), ambient and chillout music, synth and sample-constructed music (like Simple Minds and Depeche Mode), early 80s techno pop (OMD, Soft Cell), and industrial music (Nine Inch Nails). "Pick any starting point in music anytime after 1977. And you will somehow be led back in some fashion to Craftwork."

podcast.title: Consistently Excellent Live Sound (2004, 2014)
podcast.body: Kraftwerk is recognized for consistently delivering "awesome, great concert sound," with notable performances in 2004 and 2014. Their live audio quality is so refined that it is compared to "listening to an extremely good stereo system," reflecting their meticulous approach to sound. "They've always taken amazing care when it comes to their live sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Despotic" Control by Founders
podcast.body: Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider were perceived to exert a "despotic" level of control over everyone associated with Crabwork. They managed all aspects of the project, including significant creative and business decisions, often without consulting or even informing other band members. "realmente había una especie de comportamiento de espota entre Ralph Yfloria en todo lo que lo rodeaba, era como los que movían todo el engranaje de una manera un tanto de espota."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: "Fahr'n, Fahr'n" vs. "Fun, Fun, Fun"
podcast.body: On their "Autobahn" album, Kraftwerk's lyrics "Fahr'n, Fahr'n" (German for "driving") were a deliberate homage to driving, distinct from any notion of copying The Beach Boys' "Fun, Fun, Fun." This highlights their focus on a uniquely German cultural experience. "They were saying, Ferrin's Ferrin, which is German for driving. Not fun, fun, fun."

podcast.body: The band adopted a sophisticated look with suits, short hair, and sometimes ties, which stood in stark contrast to the scruffy aesthetic of punk fashion. "Crawford, for example, wore suits, had short hair, sometimes wore ties."

podcast.title: Austere Living Despite Wealth
podcast.body: Despite Crabwork generating significant income, the band members, particularly Wolfgang Fuhr, lived under remarkably austere conditions. Funds were predominantly channeled into the Kling Klang Studio, leading to modest accommodations on tour, such as sharing rooms in discreet hotels, and personal financial constraints for individuals like Wolfgang, who at times lacked money for desired purchases. "Craf Work de Aquella ganaba muchísimo dinero y que sin embargo vivían en unas condiciones increíblemente austeras."

podcast.title: Autobahn as Turning Point
podcast.body: The release of "Autobahn" in 1974 marked a significant turning point, where the band deliberately abandoned traces of rock culture to build a quasi-corporate identity. This shift involved cutting their hair, adopting suits and ties, and cultivating a retro-futurist technocrat image that was anti-rock. "El verdadero punto de inflexión llegó con Autobahn, donde dejaron atrás cualquier rastro de la cultura rock y empezaron a construirse como una entidad casi corporativa."

podcast.body: The name "Kraftwerk" means "power station," symbolizing concepts like electricity, industry, mechanization, and automation. podcast.title: Breakup of Classical Formation Dynamics
podcast.body: The classical lineup of Crabwork ultimately dissolved due to the dominant personalities of Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider, and the overwhelming influence of the Kling Klang Studio. Karl Bartos departed out of frustration, feeling creatively stifled because much of the material he developed was not utilized. Wolfgang Fuhr also left the group, feeling dejected and diminished by the band's controlling environment. "la formación clásica de Craf Work se acababa rompiendo."

podcast.body: The band Kraftwerk was celebrated for its minimalist aesthetic and clean lines, which transcended mere fashion to become a profound art statement in itself. podcast.body: Emil Schult joined the band and is often considered the "fifth Kraftwerk." He, along with Florian Schneider, designed the band's canonical image for both albums and live performances. "Fue un encargado de ir convirtiendo poco a poco a la banda, prácticamente en robots."

podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1980s, Kraftwerk was reportedly not at its peak, symbolizing a broader downturn in the quality and output of electronic music production during that period. "a final de los 80 cravuer tampoco estaba pasando por su mejor momento por ejemplo."

podcast.title: Definition of Classical Formation
podcast.body: The band's "classical formation," traditionally recognized as Ralph Hütter, Florian Schneider, Karl Bartos, and Wolfgang Fuhr, is understood to have both started and concluded with the tenure of Wolfgang Fuhr within the group. His arrival and subsequent departure marked the boundaries of this specific lineup's existence. "normalmente consideramos que lo que llamamos la formación clásica de Crabwork, que son Ralph Florian, Carl y Wolfgang, empieza y termina con la llegada y con la marcha de Wolfgang Fuhr."

podcast.title: Detroit Techno Influence
podcast.body: In Detroit, during the emergence of techno, Kraftwerk was a primary source of inspiration, listened to alongside tracks like "Zohyfield of Demoroder." Techno pioneer Juan Atkins cited Kraftwerk, Parliament, and Funkadelic as his main influences. "En Detroit, cuando estaba gestándose el tecno, lo que más escuchaba era Crafwerk, junto al tema Zohyfield of Demoroder."

podcast.title: Difficult Period (Late 1980s-Early 1990s)
podcast.body: The band was not experiencing its best period during the late 1980s and early 1990s, which contributed to the context of Carl Bartons' departure in 1990. "Craguerda, a finales de los 80 y 30 de la 90 no estaba pasando por su mejor racha."

podcast.title: Early Influence on Belleville Three
podcast.body: The European electronic music of Kraftwerk was a crucial early influence for Juan Atkins, Derrick May, and Kevin Saunderson, contributing to their futuristic sound palette. "sobre todo música europea electrónica, Crafwer."

podcast.title: Early Sound and Evolution
podcast.body: Kraftwerk's initial phase was vastly different from their later historical image. Their first three albums featured a more psychedelic and rock-anchored sound, incorporating drums, guitar, and flutes, with members often wearing long leather coats. Florian Schneider later referred to these early works as "sonic geology." "Sus primeros tres discos tienen un sonido más, psicodélico y anclado al rock, combatería, guitarra, flautas, y un duca corde a ese sonido, pero los largos chupas de piel."

podcast.title: Electronic Krautrock Pioneers
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was an integral part of the Krautrock movement, fully embracing electronics in their music. "Some went all in with electronics like craft work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Electronic Music Pioneers and Influences
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was incredibly important and influential in the development of electronic music, with many genres and ideas flowing from their work, including Technopop, Industrial Music, and elements of Hip Hop. They were instrumental in establishing the idea that electronics were as viable as guitars for making rock and roll, and their clean, thematic approach to albums made them worthy of deep study. "Kraftwerk was incredibly important and incredibly influential when it came to the whole idea of electronic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exclusive Business Dealings During Tours
podcast.body: During a lengthy US tour, which lasted nearly a year, Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider alone handled all commercial agreements and finalized performance arrangements. They often did so without informing the other band members, leaving them unaware of the tour's duration or upcoming locations. "Ralph Yfloria anivan todo el tiempo a cerrar las actuaciones y van todo el tiempo a hacer los acuerdos comerciales sin contar con ellos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Extensive Uncredited Personnel
podcast.body: Beyond the commonly recognized four main members, Crabwork's operations involved a large, often unacknowledged group of collaborators. This included lyricists, sound engineers, industrial technicians, and experts who were instrumental in constructing the specialized musical machinery used by the band, all of whom were integral to the complex structure of Crabwork. "Tenemos a letristas, tenemos a ingenieros de sonido, tenemos a técnicos industriales, tenemos a gente que los ayudó a construir todas esas máquinas con las que desarrollaban la música."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Five-Year Hiatus
podcast.body: After consistently releasing an album almost every year since their formation, Kraftwerk experienced a five-year hiatus between "Tour de France" (1983) and "Electric Café" (1986). "vieron un parón de cinco años hasta su siguiente trabajo."

srcs.source: Central Sonora

podcast.title: Founders' Dedication and Obsession
podcast.body: The lives of Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider were entirely consumed by and dedicated to the Crabwork project. This extreme commitment manifested in their relentless focus on the Kling Klang Studio, which became the central destination for all of the band's generated income. "la vida de estos dos genios era una vida dedicada por y para el proyecto de Craf Work."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Founding Fathers of Rap Influence
podcast.body: Kraftwerk is recognized for their foundational influence on rap music, particularly through Afrika Bambaataa's sampling of their work in "Planet Rock." Their pioneering electronic sounds provided a template for future hip hop and dance genres. "And by extension, we must give respect to craft work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Members and Lineup Changes
podcast.body: Craguer was founded by Sonral and Florian. The other two members of the band changed relatively often throughout the group's history, with Carl Bartons being the only person to become a true third member for a significant period. "Craguer es un grupo fundado por dos personas de Sonral y Florian y los otros dos miembros han cambiado relativamente a menudo a lo largo de la historia del grupo."

podcast.title: From Organization to Power Plant
podcast.body: Kraftwerk emerged from the ashes of the experimental group Organization. Its name, "Kraftwerk," is German for "power plant." Founding members Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider, originally classical music students, developed a keen interest in synthesizers and began experimenting with synth and drum machine music, leading to their unique all-electronic sound. "Organization, remember that band we talked about? It became Kraftwerk, which is German for power plant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gateway via Moroder
podcast.body: For those who became interested in electronic music through the work of Giorgio Moroder, it was a relatively short step to discover and appreciate Kraftwerk. Moroder's innovative use of synthesizers served as an important entry point, leading listeners to other pioneering electronic artists like Kraftwerk. "And if you got into electronic music through Moroder, it wasn't that far a hop to craftwork."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hermetic Nature and Public Perception
podcast.body: Crabwork has consistently maintained a very private stance regarding its internal workings, offering minimal details in interviews and keeping personal lives of its members largely out of the public eye. This secrecy has fueled a considerable amount of speculative and often incorrect information written about the band, making it difficult for the public to access reliable facts about them. "Siempre han sido una banda como muy hermética dentro de lo que pasa dentro del proyecto, nunca nos han dado excesivos datos, nunca han dado entrevistas excesivamente comprometidas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Independent Production and Mastering (Transiro de Plexpress)
podcast.body: For tasks like mastering and post-production, and even initial production stages, Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider worked separately from the other band members. This was exemplified with the album "Transiro de Plexpress," where they traveled to the United States for these processes, and Karl Bartos only saw the finished, manufactured version of the album. "Ralph Yfloria se irán separados para hacerla sin contar con el resto de miembros de la banda."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Influence and Legacy
podcast.body: Kraftwerk is recognized as one of the most influential and mysterious bands in modern music, fundamentally changing the language of music by reinventing composition, reprogramming new sounds, and redefining musical representation. Their influence is evident in genres like techno, industrial, synth-pop, progressive rock, post-punk, and hip-hop. "una de las bandas más influyentes y misteriosas de la música moderna."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Influence of German Identity
podcast.body: Growing up in post-World War II Germany, with a complex and "confused sense of identity" exacerbated by the denazification period, young musicians like Kraftwerk aimed to forge a new musical identity. Their goal was to create music not beholden to American or UK influences, leading them to embrace the modern electronic music of their homeland, often abandoning traditional rock instrumentation. "Their goal came to be the creation of a new form of music that wasn't beholden to what was happening in America or the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on American Black Music
podcast.body: Despite their disciplined, austere, and industrial German aesthetic, Kraftwerk left a profound mark on the passionate and physical Black American music scene, including electro, hip-hop, and Miami Bass. "acabará dejando una huella tan profunda en la música negrasta de un idiense, mucho más pasional y corporal."

srcs.source: Central Sonora

podcast.title: Influence on Avant-garde Punk
podcast.body: Kraftwerk's "primitive electronic" music (referred to as "crowdwork" in the transcript) was a significant reference for the avant-garde faction of punk, who sought new paths beyond traditional rock and roll. "en la electrónica primitiva de crowdwork"

podcast.title: Influence on Aviador Dro
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was one of the international electronic music pioneers whose work influenced Aviador Dro, the pioneers of electronic pop in Spain. Their impact helped define Aviador Dro's sound. "tomó influencias de bandas como de Residence, Divo o Crafwerk."

podcast.title: Influence on Bowie's Berlin Period
podcast.body: Kraftwerk, along with other krautrock bands like Can and Neu!, deeply fascinated David Bowie by 1977. Their electronic music and German krautrock sound heavily influenced Bowie's "Berlin period," where he sought to shed his popstar image and explore new musical territories. "He had also grown fascinated with electronic music and German crowd rock, bands like Cannes, Noy, and of course, Croftvirk."

podcast.title: Influence on David Bowie
podcast.body: David Bowie was deeply interested in Kraftwerk and the rising sound of synthesizers in Germany, which significantly influenced his musical evolution towards electronic methods of production and his move to Berlin. "He was deeply interested in what was happening in Germany with groups such as Kraftwerk, Ken, New, and the rising sound of synthesizers."

podcast.title: Influence on David Bowie's Berlin Period
podcast.body: David Bowie discovered and was hugely enamored with the electronic sounds of Kraftwerk during his time in Berlin. Their music, along with that of Neu!, significantly influenced Bowie's shift towards electronic methods of music production and contributed to the sound of his Berlin trilogy albums. "Bowie was hugely enamored with German electronic music, specifically craft work."

podcast.body: Giorgio Moroder, producer of Donna Summer's "I Feel Love," reportedly "borrowed a page from" Kraftwerk for his heavy reliance on the Moog synthesizer and electronic music production techniques. "he borrowed a page from the German Electronic Music Band craft work."

podcast.body: Kraftwerk's music heavily influenced Afrika Bambaataa, who directly sampled musical fragments from the German band in his seminal track "Planet Rock," establishing Kraftwerk as a pillar for US electronic music, modern Hip Hop, Techno, and House. "Esta canción está tan influenciada por la música alemana y por la banda crap arc que directamente tiene fragmentos musicales sacados ampliados de la banda crap arc."

podcast.body: Mogwai cites Kraftwerk as an influence. "They also like to cop ideas from Fugazi, and Kraftwerk, and Nirvana, and Electronic Offits like the Orb and the Apex Twin."

podcast.title: Influential Robotic Sound
podcast.body: Kraftwerk's music from the late 1970s, exemplified by "The Model," was characterized by a robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe. This sound was a significant part of early Technopop and greatly intrigued and influenced artists like David Bowie. "And note the vibe of that song. Much of early technopop was robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and just generally a little intense. That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kling Klang Studio
podcast.body: Kraftwerk's studio in Dusseldorf, known as Kling Klang, was the site of endless hours of experimentation that led to a string of important albums released over seven years following their 1974 album, "Autobahn." This studio became synonymous with their unique electronic sound. "resulting from the endless hours of experimenting at their studio in Dusseldorf, called Kling Kling."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legacy in the 90s
podcast.body: Despite losing some of their earlier relevance, Kraftwerk's legacy remained potent, notably influencing artists like Aphex Twin, who cited "Computer World" as an inspiration, and shaping the direction of electronic music in the 1990s. "aunque habían perdido relevancia su legado seguía vivo, marcando el rumbo de la música electrónica de los 90."

podcast.title: Live Performance in Stockholm
podcast.body: A live recording of Kraftwerk performing in Stockholm was highlighted as an example of their exceptional live sound. "Kraftwerk, live and stock home. You'll see what I mean."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Machines as Creativity
podcast.body: Unlike traditional rock, which often reacted against industrialization, Kraftwerk embraced machines as a form of creativity. They integrated themselves into industrial logic to forge a new language of resistance through music. "en vez de huir de las máquinas, las vieron como una forma de creatividad."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Pioneering Electronic Sound
podcast.body: Starting in the early 1970s, Kraftwerk, an all-electronic band from Dusseldorf, West Germany, developed cold, robotic, minimalist, futuristic, and sometimes pessimistic and dystopian sounds. Their work laid the foundational groundwork for a vast range of future music genres including technopop, industrial music, hip hop, and even disco. "Starting in the early 70s, they said about creating some cold, robotic, minimalist, futuristic, and sometimes pessimistic and dystopian sounds that would end up laying the foundations for everything from technopop to industrial music to hip hop to, yeah, even disco in the years ahead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Electronic Sounds
podcast.body: Kraftwerk pioneered the use of synthesizers to create entirely artificial sounds like square waves, which differed significantly from traditional "nice, smooth, rounded waveforms." These explorations led to the generation of unique and "very cool" sonic textures. "Instead of nice, smooth, rounded waveforms, these things could generate square waves, totally artificial sounds and very cool ones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering German Electronic Music
podcast.body: In the 1960s, West German artists like Kraftwerk sought to develop a unique musical style that diverged from American and British sounds, leading many to embrace electronic sounds. Kraftwerk emerged as the most influential among them, achieving best-selling albums and international chart success that significantly drew attention to electronic music. "But special props must go to craft work. In the 1960s, Germans, or more correctly West Germans, we're looking for a style of music that they could call their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Sound Reinterpreted
podcast.body: During their hiatus and thereafter, Kraftwerk's pioneering sound was widely reinterpreted by other artists and pushed to new commercial and experimental heights. "Su sonido pionero empezaba a ser reinterpretado por otros, y llevado nuevas cotas comerciales y experimentales."

podcast.title: Pioneering Synthesizer Use
podcast.body: Kraftwerk demonstrated how synthesizers could be utilized for purposes beyond experimental music or sound effects for planetarium shows, influencing subsequent electronic music artists. "Meanwhile, groups such as Kraftworth were demonstrating how synthesizer sounds could be used for something other than experimental music and sound effects for planetarium shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneers of Electronic Music
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was one of the artists whose pioneering electronic music was championed by David Bowie and Brian Eno in the late 1970s. "who championed the electronic music being pioneered by the likes of Croftvark and Donna Summer."

podcast.body: The introduction of the Syntanorma sequencer caused a radical stylistic change for Kraftwerk, shifting their focus from melodic synthesizer work to complex sampling and sequencing, as evidenced by albums like "Trans-Europe Express" and "Man-Machine." "Estilísticamente la banda grabar cambia radicalmente gracias a esta máquina."

podcast.title: Rejection of Collaborations
podcast.body: Kraftwerk are known for their fierce independence and consistent refusal to collaborate with other artists, a stance they maintained even when approached by major figures like David Bowie and Kanye West. Their rejection of Bowie's offer for the "Berlin Trilogy" projects underscores their unique and insular creative process. "Crabbro nunca trabaja con nadie. Me refiero a este gente muy independiente, siempre han rechazado todas las colaboraciones, han rechazado a Kanye West, han rechazado a David Bowie, han rechazado a todo el mundo."

podcast.title: Robovox Creation
podcast.body: Florian Schneider, a founding member of Kraftwerk, personally built an instrument called the Robovox. This custom-made device was used to treat vocals in a distinctive electronic way, contributing to the band's innovative sound, particularly on their 1974 "Autobahn" album. "something called a Robovox, which Florian Schneider built himself so he could treat vocals in a cool electronic way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Salaried Employment of Members
podcast.body: All individuals involved in Crabwork, including temporary members like András Hoffman and Flitch Hilbert, and even the core members of the classical formation such as Karl Bartos and Wolfgang Fuhr, were employed as salaried workers by Ralph Hütter and Florian Schneider. They received a fixed wage for their contributions to the project, highlighting the hierarchical structure. "nos cuenta Wolfanfurt que todos ellos, incluidos los otros miembros de Crabwork, incluso de la banda clásica que conocemos a Carvartos y Wolfanfurt, que eran asalariados de Ralph Yfloria."

podcast.title: Sampled in KLF Song
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was one of the artists whose material was sampled in The KLF's 1990 hit single "What Time Is Love." "There were at least eight samples in this track, including from the MC5, Kraftwerk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Serious Electronic Music
podcast.body: For Kraftwerk, electronic music was a profound artistic pursuit, not a fleeting trend. It necessitated rigorous study, advanced engineering, and the construction of new musical instruments, underscoring their commitment to evolving the genre. "The electronic music was serious business. It required study and engineering and the building of new machines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Suppression of Ego
podcast.body: The band intentionally suppressed individuality and ego, presenting themselves as a unified system rather than individual artists. "Moraron al individuo y el ego, y se presentaron como un sistema unificado."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Surpassed by Emerging Scenes
podcast.body: After their groundbreaking work with "Computer World," Kraftwerk observed various groups, producers, and scenes catching up to and even surpassing them in the mid-1980s, despite having been years ahead in the 1970s and early 1980s. "vieron como varios grupos, productores y escenas, empezaban a alcanzarlos e incluso adelantarlos."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Synthesizer Application to Pop Music
podcast.body: Kraftwerk demonstrated how synthesizers could be effectively integrated into pop music in meaningful ways. Their influence was significant for musicians inspired by punk but seeking alternatives to guitar-driven sounds, especially by the early 1980s when synthesizers became widespread. "They showed how synthesizers could be applied to pop music in meaningful ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Synthesizer Fascination
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was captivated by the cold, otherworldly sounds of the synthesizer, leading them to extensive experimentation with these new machines. They discovered that synthesizers could produce sounds previously unheard by humans, such as square waves, which they described as "totally artificial sounds and very cool ones." "Fascinated by the cold, otherworldly sounds of the synthesizer, craftwork began experimenting with the new machines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Technically Minded Group
podcast.body: Kraftwerk is noted as one of the most technically minded groups of all time, with their album "Computer World" (1981) predating the reality of artificial intelligence. The group is still active and potentially experimenting with new technologies in their "sonic lab," continuing their legacy of incorporating advanced tech into their music. "Craftwork, one of the most technically minded groups of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History and Future of AI in Music

podcast.title: Teutonic Discipline and Image
podcast.body: Kraftwerk adopted a profoundly German, Teutonic, and austere discipline, which served as an image of unity for the band. They were admired for their determination to differentiate themselves from American sequences and chords, and to break away from the traditional rock image. "adoptaron esa disciplina teotónica y austera como una imagen de unidad."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Transcending Borders
podcast.body: Kraftwerk's music quickly transcended geographical and cultural borders, finding unexpected resonance with diverse sensibilities worldwide. "Son música no tardó entre los pasados fronteras."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Tribute in Bowie's "Heroes" Album
podcast.body: Florian Schneider, one of the founders of Kraftwerk, was honored with a tribute on David Bowie's "Heroes" album. A song on the record, "V2 Schneider," was named in his recognition. "There's also a song in the record called V2 Schneider which is not too florean Schneider, one of the founders of Kraftwerk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: US Recognition (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: While Krautrock generally had limited diffusion outside Europe in the late 1970s, Kraftwerk was an exception, being known by many people in the United States, although this did not translate into a widespread "hype" or consistent chart positioning for the genre.

podcast.title: Visual Style Influence
podcast.body: Kraftwerk's distinctive electronic sound inspired a corresponding visual aesthetic. Unlike the disheveled appearance of punks, their look featured sharp suits, ties, and meticulously groomed hair, projecting a cold and detached image. "This sound spawned a look. No scruffy punks here. Like war, sharpsuits and ties and had perfectly groomed hair."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Volkswagen Beetle Samples
podcast.body: Some of the unique sounds on Kraftwerk's track "Autobahn" were sourced from Ralf Hütter's Volkswagen Beetle. These sounds were captured by a tape recorder hanging out the window during a drive down the A555 autobahn, which links Bonn and Cologne, a major center for electronic music experimentation at the time. "Some of the sounds on this track are taken from Ralph Hooder's Volkswagen Beetle, captured by a taper quarter hanging out the window on a way down their highway called the A555."

xref.body: The Beatles were recognized as a major influence on young German musicians, alongside other British and American acts, but German artists ultimately sought to create something different rather than merely imitating them. This band is also cited as arguably the second most influential band in history after Kraftwerk. "It wasn't good enough just to imitate the Beatles of the Stones, something else, something different was required."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Berlin Move and Addiction Recovery
xref.body: To recover from his drug addiction and escape the intense spotlight of Los Angeles, David Bowie decided to move away. After a temporary stop in Switzerland, he relocated to Berlin with his friend Iggy Pop. "Para recuperarse y escapar del foco de atención, decide huir de los ángeles que su amigo y hip-hop."

srcs.source: Central Sonora

xref.title: Deeter Character Inspiration
xref.body: Mike Myers was inspired to create the character Deeter from the "Sprockets" sketch on Saturday Night Live by observing a waiter at a venue called the Camerunhouse in Toronto. The sketch also featured a Kraftwerk song played at the wrong speed as its theme, and Deeter's monkey, Klaus, was named after avant-garde singer Klaus Nomi. "Lord has it that Mike Myers was inspired to create Deeter by a waiter at a venue called the Camerunhouse in Toronto."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early German Electronic Musicians
xref.body: Tangerine Dream was among the German groups that began creating electronic music in the early 1970s, seeking to establish a unique musical identity separate from the prevailing British and American rock and roll. This development was significantly aided by the experimental electronic studio built by West German Radio, which had exposed German musicians to electronic sounds for nearly two decades. "There were groups like Cannes and Tangerine Dream, and most important of all, Kraftwerk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Echoing Kraftwerk
xref.body: Coldplay deliberately echoed Kraftwerk's style in a 2005 song, which became a major hit single globally. This direct influence led to Kraftwerk receiving songwriting credits for the track, contributing to the "X&Y" album's sales of over 15 million copies. "Here's Coldplay, deliberately echoing Craftwork in 2005. And before you ask, yes, Craftwork does get songwriting credits on this Coldplay song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Evolution to Electronic Sound
xref.body: Initially resembling Joy Division with dark, guitar-driven music, New Order quickly embraced synth pop sounds, drawing inspiration from Kraftwerk and other German bands. Over time, they incorporated more electronics, drum machines, synthesizers, and samplers, moving towards a more electronic sound. "But they very soon started bringing in synth pop sounds that owed more to a nod to craftwork and a few other German bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fascination and Adoption of Synthesizers
xref.body: David Bowie was deeply fascinated by the electronic music Kraftwerk was creating and quickly immersed himself in using synthesizers. His embrace of this technology captured public attention and contributed to the wider acceptance of electronic sounds in popular music. "David Bowie was fascinated by what craft work was doing and immediately dove into synthesizers and that got people's attention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Founding Father of Rap
xref.body: Afrika Bambaataa is widely recognized as one of the founding fathers of rap, particularly for his influential track "Planet Rock." This song's innovative use of electronic sounds and sampling, including a Kraftwerk sample, profoundly shaped the direction of hip hop and related genres. "And he is recognized as one of the founding fathers of rap."

xref.title: Influenced Major Artists
xref.body: The Velvet Underground is credited with awakening and influencing a wide array of prominent artists and bands, including David Bowie, Roxy Music, The Doors, Patti Smith, Iggy Pop and the Stooges, U2, Joy Division, The Pixies, The Sex Pistols, Talking Heads, The Cure, Kraftwerk, R.E.M., Simple Minds, The Strokes, and The Psychedelic Furs, whose name derived from a Velvet Underground song. "Here is a list of just some of the few who claimed to have been awakened by the velvet underground and then incorporated some of whatever they were doing into their music."

xref.title: Influenced by Bowie and Kraftwerk
xref.body: Miller was influenced by the electronic music of David Bowie and Kraftwerk, combining the concept of stylish, futuristic, machine-generated music with punk rock's DIY aesthetic. "Like a number of young British musicians, Miller had been exposed to craft work and the electronic musings of David Bowie."

xref.title: Influences
xref.body: Mogwai is highly influenced by a diverse range of artists including post-punk bands like Joy Division, Sonic Youth, and My Bloody Valentine, as well as Fugazi, Kraftwerk, Nirvana, and electronic artists like The Orb and Aphex Twin. "The guys in Mug-Y are highly influenced by post-punk bands, like Jordy Vision, Sonic Youth, and my Bloody Valentine. They also like to cop ideas from Fugazi, and Kraftwerk, and Nirvana, and Electronic Offits like the Orb and the Apex Twin."

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Underworld, a prominent group in EDM and techno, is directly linked to Kraftwerk's influence, illustrating how the German pioneers laid foundational groundwork for these electronic genres. "Today's EDM and all techno from groups like Underworld and anything that came out of Detroit to Daff Punk, Ambient and Chillout music, Craftwork influence."

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Daft Punk's music, particularly within EDM and techno, is cited as being under the influence of Kraftwerk, showcasing the enduring impact of the German band on contemporary electronic music. "Today's EDM and all techno from groups like Underworld and anything that came out of Detroit to Daff Punk, Ambient and Chillout music, Craftwork influence."

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Simple Minds is mentioned as one of the bands influenced by Kraftwerk's approach to synth and sample-constructed music, highlighting the German group's role in shaping the sound of early electronic pop. "Many synth and sample constructed music running from simple minds to Depesh Mode. Craftwork."

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Depeche Mode is cited as a group whose synth and sample-constructed music was influenced by Kraftwerk, underscoring the German pioneers' foundational role in the development of electronic music and synth-pop. "Many synth and sample constructed music running from simple minds to Depesh Mode. Craftwork."

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Soft Cell, an early 80s techno pop act, is identified as having been influenced by Kraftwerk, demonstrating the German band's widespread reach in shaping the electronic music landscape. "Early 80s techno pop like OMD and Soft Cell. Craftwork."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Nine Inch Nails, a key band in industrial music, is mentioned as being influenced by Kraftwerk. This illustrates how Kraftwerk's experimental electronic sound extended its impact into more abrasive and boundary-pushing genres from the late 1970s onwards. "Industrial music starting in the late 70s and going through 9-inch nails and beyond. Craftwork."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kraftwerk Influence
xref.body: Bowie's three albums created in Berlin with Brian Eno were explicitly "Kraftwerk inspired." These works showcased a belief that electronics represented a viable and important path forward for musical innovation. "He created three craftwork inspired albums with producer Brian Eno that show that maybe electronics were the way for."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Krautrock and Berlin Influence
xref.body: David Bowie was profoundly "shaken and inspired" by early Krautrock, especially Kraftwerk, which led him to move to Berlin. This period resulted in three of his most fascinating albums: "Low," "Heroes," and "Lodger," with the B-side of the "Heroes" single, "V-2 Schneider," directly named after Florian Schneider. "David Bowie was so shaken and inspired by early crop rock and craftwork in particular, as he moved to Berlin and made three of his most fascinating albums as a result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Move to West Berlin with Iggy Pop
xref.body: Deeply influenced by German electronic groups like Kraftwerk, Can, and Neu!, and envisioning electronic music as the future, Bowie moved to West Berlin with Iggy Pop to immerse themselves in the local scene and simultaneously recover from their addictions. They settled in a modest place at Hopstresser 155 in the Schöneberg area, motivated by a belief that remaining in Los Angeles would lead to their demise. "He began to think that these electronic methods of producing music were the future. And what better way to follow this muse than to move to where it all seemed to be happening? Germany."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneer of Hip Hop
xref.body: Afrika Bambaataa is recognized as one of the most influential early rappers, DJs, and hip hop producers, credited with coming up with breakbeat dancing. His work, particularly "Planet Rock," directly leveraged the influential beats from Kraftwerk's "Trans-Europe Express," solidifying Kraftwerk's foundational role in hip hop. "Now, here's Africa Vambada, one of the most influential of all the early rappers DJs and hip hop producers. He's one of the people who came up with breakbeat dancing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Predecessor to Kraftwerk
xref.body: Organization was an early Krautrock group that broke up after releasing their challenging 1970 album, "Tone Float." Out of its ashes, a brand new and arguably one of the most influential bands in the history of rock, Kraftwerk, was formed. "organization broke up. But out of its ashes came a brand new group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robotic Electronic Experiments
xref.body: Some of David Bowie's electronic experiments exhibited a similar robotic, cold, artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe to early Technopop artists like Kraftwerk and The Normal. This aesthetic characterized a significant portion of the emerging electronic music scene. "That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sampled in KLF Song
xref.body: The Doors' music was among the various samples incorporated into The KLF's influential 1990 single, "What Time Is Love." "There were at least eight samples in this track, including from the MC5, Kraftwerk, the doors."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Synth Experimentation and Production
xref.body: Giorgio Moroder, an Italian musician, was a pioneer in experimenting with new synthesizers as they emerged. His work, particularly his production of Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" in 1977, was highly influential, shaping the sound of disco with robotic, futuristic elements and inspiring countless electronic and technopop bands. Moroder's innovations drew a direct line to groups like Depeche Mode, OMD, and the Human League, and even inspired David Bowie, serving as a gateway to electronic music and Kraftwerk for many fans. "He had an extraordinarily big hit in 1977 with this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Upbeat Electronic Pop
xref.body: Their first single, released in May 1979, showcased a unique style of electronic pop music that, unlike Kraftwerk's sound, was upbeat, happy, and described as "holds full." "Not only was their music completely electronic, but unlike craftwork, OMD's band of pop music was upbeat, happy, and there we say it. Holds full."
